common_name: Red Long-Headed Coneflower (Solid Mahogany-Red Prairie Coneflower)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or early spring on dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; like the species, var. pulcherrima flowers reliably from first-year seedlings and prefers poor soil, since excess fertility leads to weak, floppy stems.

directions: Ratibida columnifera var. pulcherrima is a naturally occurring, solid mahogany-red-flowered form of prairie coneflower that arises within wild populations across the Great Plains and is now selected and offered in the native seed trade for gardeners wanting a richer, more saturated color mass than the typical bicolor species. It shares the same tall, cylindrical, thimble-shaped central cone and the same elongated 'long-headed' silhouette as the species, but the drooping ray petals are a uniform deep brick-red to burgundy rather than yellow-tipped, giving plantings a warmer overall color from a distance. It carries the same deep taproot, drought tolerance, and adaptability to poor, lean, well-drained soils that make prairie coneflower one of the toughest native prairie wildflowers, and self-seeding populations gradually produce a mix of red and red-and-yellow offspring over time. Combine with the straight yellow species or with native grasses for a richly colored, low-water meadow planting.

common_name: Sticky Rosinweed (Bibb County Dolomite Glade Endemic)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification in well-drained, gravelly, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sticky rosinweed is a rare Bibb County, Alabama dolomite-glade endemic that resents transplanting once its taproot is set.

directions: Sticky rosinweed is a rare Alabama endemic restricted to the dolomite glades of Bibb County, where thin, gravelly, alkaline soil and full sun create the harsh, exposed conditions this deep-taprooted Silphium is adapted to withstand. Its stems, leaves, and flower bracts are covered in short, stalked, amber glandular hairs that give the whole plant a noticeably sticky, resinous feel unlike any of its rosinweed relatives. From July into August it sends up branching stalks bearing soft yellow, daisy-like composite flowers above broad, coarse-textured basal leaves, drawing specialist bees and other pollinators during the height of summer. Because it was only formally described in 2001 and remains imperiled in the wild, sticky rosinweed is grown mainly by native plant specialists and botanical gardens working to conserve Alabama's unique Ketona dolomite flora, and like other Silphium it resents transplanting once its taproot is established.

planting.note: Direct sow on the soil surface in fall for natural cold stratification in well-drained, calcareous, lean to average soil in full sun; cutleaf prairie dock is uncommon in cultivation and resents transplanting once its deep taproot is established.

directions: Cutleaf prairie dock is a rare native of limestone prairies, barrens, and cedar glades in Alabama, Georgia, Kentucky, and Tennessee, distinguished from the more familiar prairie dock (Silphium terebinthinaceum) by its deeply pinnately lobed, almost fern-cut basal leaves rather than that species' broad, unlobed leaves. From a basket-sized rosette of foliage, a smooth, nearly leafless flowering stalk rises dramatically through summer, eventually topped by loose clusters of yellow, sunflower-like composite blooms that draw native bees and other pollinators into early fall. Like other Silphium, it invests years of growth into a deep taproot before flowering and becomes extremely long-lived, drought-tolerant, and essentially maintenance-free once established, but it strongly resents being transplanted after its first year in the ground. Its striking cut-leaf foliage and towering bloom stalk make it a dramatic textural accent for native limestone-glade or prairie-style plantings within its home range.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Carolina green-and-gold is native to the southern Appalachians and western Piedmont and spreads at a modest, intermediate pace compared to other varieties.

directions: Carolina green-and-gold is the southern mountain variety of the familiar woodland groundcover, found from the Carolinas and Georgia west to Alabama, Tennessee, and Kentucky in the southern Appalachians and western Piedmont, where it grows in rich deciduous woodland understory and along shaded slopes. It differs from the typical clumping variety and from the far-running coastal-plain variety (var. australe) by producing short stolons only one to two and a half inches long, giving it an intermediate spreading habit that still eventually knits together into mats up to two feet across without becoming aggressive. Bright, five-petaled, star-shaped yellow flowers rise just above the low, scalloped foliage from mid-spring into early summer, providing early nectar for small native bees along the woodland edge. It is a good choice for gardeners within its native mountain range who want the ecological authenticity of a true local ecotype rather than a coastal or piedmont-selected cultivar.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; 'Mark Viette' stays in a tight, non-running clump rather than spreading by stolons.

directions: Mark Viette is a compact, clump-forming selection of green-and-gold named for the Virginia horticulturist and nurseryman, distinguished from spreading forms like Allen Bush and Eco Lacquered Spider by staying in a tight, non-running clump rather than colonizing by stolons. Thick, semi-evergreen, deep green leaves set off perky, inch-wide, buttercup-yellow flowers that open intermittently from spring through the whole summer rather than concentrating bloom into a single spring flush. Because it does not spread aggressively, it is well suited to small woodland borders, rock gardens, and mixed perennial beds where a running groundcover would be unwelcome. It performs best in light shade to nearly full sun in cooler parts of its zone 5-9 range but appreciates afternoon shade in the hotter parts of its range.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or fall in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; 'Quinn's Gold' forms slowly spreading evergreen rosettes best sited where its color-shifting blooms can be seen up close.

directions: Quinn's Gold is a patented green-and-gold selection discovered in 1998 in a Pittsboro, North Carolina garden and introduced by Niche Gardens, prized for a flower color that shifts as each bloom ages, opening a bright, saturated gold and fading through soft yellow to creamy white, so that a single plant in bloom displays several flower shades at once. Evergreen rosettes send up semi-upright flowering stalks beginning in mid-spring, forming a low mat roughly six inches tall and spreading to about two feet wide over time. Like other named green-and-gold selections it thrives in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade, blooming heavily in spring with sporadic rebloom through the rest of the growing season. The multicolored bloom effect makes it a standout among green-and-gold cultivars for gardeners who want more visual complexity than the solid-yellow species and other selections provide.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun; New England groundsel grows naturally in fens, wet meadows, and streamside swamps of eastern Canada, New England, and a few high-elevation southern Appalachian sites.

directions: New England groundsel is the cold-hardy, far-northern counterpart to golden groundsel (Packera aurea), native to eastern Canada and the New England states with a few disjunct populations surviving at high elevation on Roan Mountain along the North Carolina-Tennessee line. It forms loose, occasionally rhizomatous clumps of basal foliage and sends up flowering stems from a few inches to over two feet tall, bearing clusters of bright yellow daisy flowers from May into July. Unlike shade-loving Packera aurea, this species is found naturally in sunny, consistently moist to wet, acidic habitats such as fens, wet meadows, and streamside swamps, making it a good choice for a sunny rain garden or pond margin in its cold-hardy native range. It provides the same early-season nectar and pollen value for small native bees as its better-known southern relatives, and should not be confused with any invasive Old World groundsel species.
